blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a USENIX Security 2018 Distinguished Paper that evaluates browser defenses against third-party cookie tracking and cross-site attacks. The paper systematically tests seven major browsers and 46 extensions, finding that every combination has vulnerabilities allowing bypass of intended security policies. The authors identify seven categories of cross-site request mechanisms (e.g., HTML tags, JavaScript APIs, PDF JavaScript) and demonstrate how these can be exploited to send cookies or initiate authenticated requests despite protections like same-site cookies. Notably, PDF JavaScript in Chrome/Opera and redirect-based bypasses in Safari were particularly effective. The study also reveals flaws in all tested ad-blocking and tracking protection extensions, often due to developers overlooking WebSocket protocols. The paper argues for a unified testing framework to detect such bypasses and proposes future work on mobile browsers and other policy mechanisms like Local Storage API.
paper_title: Who left open the cookie jar? A comprehensive evaluation of third-party cookie policies
paper_abstract: Nowadays, cookies are the most prominent mechanism to identify and authenticate users on the Internet. Although protected by the Same Origin Policy, popular browsers include cookies in all requests, even when these are cross-site. Unfortunately, these third-party cookies enable both cross-site attacks and third-party tracking. As a response to these nefarious consequences, various countermeasures have been developed in the form of browser extensions or even protection mechanisms that are built directly into the browser. In this paper, we evaluate the effectiveness of these defense mechanisms by leveraging a framework that automatically evaluates the enforcement of the policies imposed to third-party requests. By applying our framework, which generates a comprehensive set of test cases covering various web mechanisms, we identify several flaws in the policy implementations of the 7 browsers and 46 browser extensions that were evaluated. We find that even built-in protection mechanisms can be circumvented by multiple novel techniques we discover. Based on these results, we argue that our proposed framework is a much-needed tool to detect bypasses and evaluate solutions to the exposed leaks. Finally, we analyze the origin of the identified bypass techniques, and find that these are due to a variety of implementation, configuration and design flaws.
